summary: Moroccan carrot salad from Ellen Kanner's Feeding the Hungry Ghost: shredded or matchstick carrots dressed with cumin, paprika and cayenne bloomed in olive oil, lemon juice, agave or honey and salt, with parsley stirred in just before serving; 18 minutes.
glance: Prep 15 min, cook 3 min, total 18 min
1 pound, coarsely shredded or cut in 1/4-inch matchsticks
up to a day in an airtight container in the refrigerator (stir in the parsley just before serving)
faq: What is Feeding the Hungry Ghost?

A cookbook by Ellen Kanner. A hungry ghost, in Taoist theology, is a restless soul still seeking what it missed out on in life, and Kanner's thesis is that we all are in some way, wanting both physical nourishment and a deeper sense of connection from food. The author calls her exuberant and utterly not preachy.
What are the recipes in the book like?
Most contain relatively few ingredients, mostly easy-to-find staples. The author says Ellen has the gift of simplicity with food, such as her green gumbo or farinata.
How do you make the Moroccan carrot salad?

Shred or cut 1 pound of carrots into matchsticks. Heat the oil, cumin, paprika and cayenne over low heat 2 to 3 minutes until the spices darken and turn fragrant, cool, pour over the carrots, then add agave or honey, lemon juice and sea salt and stir to coat. Stir in the parsley just before serving.
Which paprika should I use?
Sweet paprika is traditional; smoked is edgy but quite nice.
How should I serve it?
Chilled but not gelid. The salad keeps in an airtight container in the refrigerator for a day.

summary: Ethiopian-style chard with berbere: onion and garlic fried 2 minutes, 1 to 3 tablespoons of berbere bloomed for 10 seconds, then damp chard with its stems covered about 10 minutes until wilted; 10 minutes of active work.
glance: about 10 minutes active, plus about 10 minutes covered
Vegetarian and gluten-free; vegan with oil instead of butter
faq: What is berbere?

The quintessential Ethiopian spice mixture, great to have in your pantry because it adds complex spice and heat to any basic preparation of vegetables. Besides chiles it can contain ginger, cloves, coriander, allspice, and less familiar flavors like long pepper, ajwain and rue.
Where do I find berbere?
At an Ethiopian grocery, or buy it online, or make your own.
Is this authentic?
The author calls it Ethiopian-style rather than authentic, because he hasn't seen chard prepared exactly this way, though it fit well in a meal with traditional dishes and injera.
Can I use the chard stems?
Yes. Don't throw them out: when cooked through they are succulent and delicious.
Why leave the chard damp?
Washing it and leaving it damp provides the moisture to wilt the greens; add a couple of tablespoons of water if needed, cover about 10 minutes, then remove the lid and cook off the remaining water.
Why chard for berbere?
Chard is a great option for folks who don't love stronger-tasting greens like mustard, collard or kale, though you can experiment with those.

summary: Homemade breadcrumbs: stale bread grated in a food processor, chopped to the texture you want and toasted about 10 minutes in olive oil and a little salt in a skillet over medium-low heat; makes 2 cups in 15 minutes.
glance: 6 thick slices of stale, not moldy, bread, crust on
very well in the freezer; re-toast to revive the crunch
faq: How do you make homemade breadcrumbs?

Grate dried-out bread in a food processor with the grating blade, switch to the chopping blade and process to the texture you want, then toast the crumbs with olive oil and a little salt in a skillet over medium-low heat, stirring frequently, until well browned and crispy, about 10 minutes.
How coarse should they be?
The author likes them fairly coarse for general use and rather fine if being used for breading.
Can I make them without stale bread?
In a pinch, slice soft bread, toast it, and let it sit about 15 minutes to dry out so it can be grated.
How do I store breadcrumbs?
They keep very well in the freezer. Give them a quick re-toast in a skillet or toaster oven to revive their crunch.
How can I flavor them?
Add crushed garlic or hearty herbs like rosemary or sage to the olive oil.
What do I use breadcrumbs for?
To top a gratin, add body to a filling, or bread a fritter.

mushroom juice plus 1/4 its volume of sweet vermouth or red wine, simmered slightly reduced

summary: Crisp polenta cakes with braised cabbage: cabbage braised about 40 minutes with cider vinegar and sugar, leftover chilled polenta patties fried until crunchy, white beans, and an ale, mustard and caraway pan sauce whisked with butter; serves 4.
glance: about 40 minutes on very low heat, vinegar and sugar added halfway
3 cups leftover polenta chilled overnight, formed into 8 patties about 5 inches across and 1/3 inch thick
6 ounces ale, caraway, Dijon mustard and butter
faq: How do you get polenta really crispy?

Cook the polenta cakes long enough and hot enough to develop a crunch, pressing the patties flat in a well-oiled pan for maximum surface area and frying until quite well browned on one side before flipping. Otherwise you'll be eating soft-on-soft mush.
How do I make the polenta ahead?
Make polenta with fennel and apples the day before and pour the extra into a lightly oiled rectangular or square baking dish, cover with plastic wrap and chill. It's easy to slice the next day.
How do you braise the cabbage?

Fry the onion 30 seconds and the cabbage 5 minutes in olive oil in a large non-cast-iron skillet, then reduce to very low with a cup of water and salt, cover and cook about 40 minutes, adding cider vinegar and sugar about halfway.
What can I use instead of ale?
The author used an apricot ale; a darker beer or white wine also work. For red cabbage use red wine with a wine vinegar or red-fruit vinegar instead of apple cider vinegar.
How do I make the pan sauce?
In the cabbage skillet, simmer the beer, mustard, caraway and a pinch of salt, whisk in butter one cube at a time, and cook it down until it lightly coats a spoon.
What does this dish feel like?
Like it would come from far northern Italy near the Austrian border; the recipe isn't precise, so taste and use your cooking common sense.

summary: Strata with caramelized onions, mushrooms and smoked mozzarella: bread cubes soaked in an egg and milk custard with tarragon and nutmeg, baked at 350°F for about 40 minutes in a 9x11 dish; it can be assembled the night before and serves 6.
glance: 350°F for about 40 minutes, until set and lightly browned
4 medium, caramelized about an hour for a generous cup
assemble the night before, refrigerate, add about 10 minutes baking from cold
faq: What is a strata?
A baked egg dish filled with cubes of bread and whatever you can muster, with all the appeal of quiche but without the slight hassle of pie crust.
Why is strata easier than quiche?
The starch from the bread tends to stabilize the custard, so there's a wider safety margin between unset eggs and overcooked, rubbery eggs.
Can I make strata the night before?
Yes. Assemble the whole dish, refrigerate it, and bake it in the morning, allowing about 10 minutes extra when baking from cold; don't preheat the oven in advance.
How do I know when strata is done?

The custard is set and the top lightly browned, about 40 minutes at 350°F. It should feel reasonably firm in the center with no jiggle, but don't overbake or the eggs can become grainy. Cool at least 10 minutes.
How long do the caramelized onions take?
About an hour: cook 4 medium sliced onions in butter over medium-low heat, lowering the heat partway through to avoid burning, for about a generous cup.

summary: Chevre with sauteed grapes and fresh herbs: 8 balls of fresh goat cheese warmed toward room temperature, topped with seedless red grapes sauteed 30 seconds in olive oil, chives, chive blossoms, oregano and flaky salt; ready in minutes.
glance: 8 ounces fresh chevre, rolled in 8 balls
1 1/2 cups halved seedless red grapes, sauteed 30 seconds
faq: Where does the idea come from?
It's a riff on a popular dish from Seattle's Osteria La Spiga, which uses Toma cheese wrapped in grape leaves. This version is even simpler.
Can I use other cheeses or herbs?
Yes. Mint or basil would be delicious, and grilled halloumi cheese could replace the chevre.
How long do I saute the grapes?
Just before serving, saute them in 1 tablespoon of olive oil over medium-high heat for 30 seconds, then distribute them warm over the cheese.
How do I serve it?
Family style or in individual portions, with a crusty baguette or grilled flatbread.
Is it vegan?
It is vegetarian and gluten-free, not vegan.

summary: Moist, intensely corny cornbread with browned butter: 1 cup stoneground cornmeal to 1 cup all-purpose flour, buttermilk and browned butter pushed through a sieve, baked in an 8x8 pan at 375°F for about 25 minutes; muffins take about 18.
glance: one 8x8-inch pan, enough for 4 for dinner (or 10 muffins)
50% cornmeal, for corn flavor without being crumbly
cook 5-10 minutes until light brown and nutty, keeping the milk solids
yield: one 8x8-inch pan, enough for 4 for dinner
faq: What makes this cornbread special?

The butter is browned before it goes into the batter, a trick the author learned from The Recipe Girl, which adds some of the umami flavor others get from bacon drippings. For extra flavor, add a tablespoon of non-fat milk powder to the butter while it browns.
What corn to wheat ratio is best?
The author likes anything 50% corn and above for mostly corn flavor; ratios range from 100% to 25%. Too much corn is tasty but very crumbly, while 50% is moist without turning into cake.
What cornmeal should I use?
The freshest, best-quality organic stoneground cornmeal you can find, preferably a coarse grind.
Can I add corn kernels, cheddar or jalapenos?
Yes, fold inclusions in just before baking, though the author prefers pure cornbread with a big pat of sweet cream butter.
What if I don't have buttermilk?
Use 3/4 cup of milk plus 1 tablespoon of white vinegar. Skim milk works okay, though you may need a little more; a full cup of milk is too liquid.
Can I bake it in muffins or a skillet?
It makes 10 muffins in about 18 minutes, and a double batch bakes beautifully in a 12-inch cast iron skillet.

summary: Quick marinated feta: a dressing of olive oil, garlic, Aleppo pepper, orange zest and fresh mint poured over a 7-ounce block of feta and served at cool room temperature with lightly toasted pita rounds.
glance: 2 tablespoons olive oil, garlic, Aleppo pepper, 1 teaspoon orange zest, 8 mint leaves
at cool room temperature with 3 lightly toasted pitas
faq: Is this really marinated?

The author calls it marinated by convention, but it is really more "dressed": the dressing doesn't sink into the cheese. Diners spread the cheese and dressing onto the pita and the flavors come together on the palate.
Why serve feta at room temperature?
Pat off surface moisture and let it come up to a cool room temperature, because cheese served at refrigerator temperature has much of its flavor muted.
What is Aleppo pepper?
A pepper grown in what used to be the Jewish part of Syria, with a gorgeous dark red color and an earthy, robust, slightly fruity flavor. If you can't find it, use regular chili flakes.
Can I use dried mint?
Yes. A more typical Middle Eastern marinade would use dried mint: 1 teaspoon, rubbed to release flavor. The flavor is quite different from fresh but equally interesting.
Which feta should I buy?
It's worth exploring varieties, such as creamy Bulgarian, French sheepsmilk or domestic brands; the author mentions the one from Mt. Vikos at Whole Foods.

summary: Red curry delicata squash and tofu: a homemade red curry paste (dried New Mexico chiles, lemongrass, ginger, garlic, lime) blended, then 5 tablespoons fried with browned tofu and half-moons of delicata squash, covered about 10 minutes with broccoli; makes extra paste to freeze.
glance: squash about 10 minutes covered; chile pods soak 20 minutes for the paste
use 5 tablespoons now, freeze the rest in portions
faq: Why put winter squash in a Thai-style curry?
The author learned of it from a terrific pumpkin curry at his favorite local Thai place. Delicata is relatively easy to cut and peel, cooks quickly and has a rich, sweet flavor.
Can I use store-bought curry paste?
In a pinch, yes, for the squash part of the recipe, but make sure it is vegetarian if that matters. Homemade paste has volatile aroma and flavor miles beyond the packaged stuff.
What do I do with extra curry paste?
The recipe makes more than one meal needs. Freeze the excess, ideally in individual portions, for curry fried rice, or a soup like laksa or khao soi.
Is this a saucy curry?
A relatively dry one: no coconut milk is added, though it has a small amount of glossy sauce, so add just a little water if needed. Serve it with jasmine rice and maybe an herb-filled salad.
How do I control the heat in the paste?
If you like your curries hot, keep the seeds and ribs of the chile pods; if not, throw them out.
